ODT (i.e., microtransit) within an AMD will use fleets of light- to medium-duty vehicles in which each vehicle is individually dispatched to pick up a party and transport them directly to their destination drop-off location without making any other “fixed-station” stops in between. This type of service is similar to TNCs, which typically provide on-demand, single-party, curb- to-curb service. TNCs also offer pooled rides in some locations, which was more common before the COVID-19 pandemic—though it is reemerging in a few places. Typically, ODT is inherently shared, without the ability to opt out of pooled ride options (as in TNCs). If additional passengers are heading in the same direction or to the same location, ODT will automatically pool the ride requests and route accordingly. As such, an ODT ride may include intermediate stops for either passenger pickup or drop-off while providing direct origin-to-destination service. Even with pooling compulsory with ODT, many trips within an ODT system remain single party, particularly during nonpeak times. The continued rapid adoption of ODT services in the United States and anticipated use of AV fleets to provide ODT have multiple operational implications for AMDs. Two of these are the design of safe, high-capacity boarding and alighting areas (stations or PUDO zones) and the implications of electrifying the fleet of light-duty, minivan-sized vehicles that typically provide ODT service. An additional operational concern for shared rides is ensuring security without the presence of a driver—an area of research slated for Phase IV. As ODT applications multiply in the United States, the need for safe and efficient passenger boarding and alighting have led to the increasing practice of predesignating specific ODT access locations. These are not traditional transit stations but often specific curbside locations that have been selected to allow a safe interface for passenger transfer to and from the vehicle as well as easily recognized landmarks for rendezvous between the passenger and vehicle. Passengers booking a pickup via a smartphone app are instructed to walk to these designated locations for service, a practice that has recently been called “corner-to-corner” service, as compared to “curb- to-curb.” The concept of a transit service providing a direct origin-to-destination service using optimized routing for each person’s travel needs is not new in the world of automated people mover systems. Such service harkens back to the concept of “personal rapid transit” (historically called by its acronym PRT) over the last 50 years, which provides direct origin-to-destination service for riders but on a dedicated guideway. More recently the PRT concept was captured by the term automated transit network (ATN), which encompasses the service concept of PRT but is more encompassing of various technologies, even including AV fleets on public rights-of-way.
